title: Active Object Pattern
oneLiner: Decouples calling a method from executing it, by queueing the request and running it later on the object's own thread.

hero.name: The Scheduler
hero.catchphrase: Call me anytime. I'll do it on my own time, in my own thread.
hero.power: Accepts method calls instantly, queues them, and executes them asynchronously on its own dedicated thread — returning a future the caller can wait on.
hero.weakness: Queueing, scheduling, and synchronization are real complexity — worth it only when concurrent access is an actual, measured problem.
hero.origin: The Scheduler appeared after a UI thread froze for two seconds every time a background image filter ran directly on it, blocking every click and keystroke.

story.problem: `imageProcessor.applyFilter(image)` runs directly on the UI thread, freezing the entire interface for two seconds on every call. Users can't click anything while it runs.
story.solution: The Scheduler turns ImageProcessor into an Active Object: `applyFilter()` just enqueues the request and returns a future immediately. A dedicated worker thread pulls requests off the queue and runs them.
story.result: The UI thread never blocks. `applyFilter()` returns instantly with a future; the actual filtering happens on its own thread, and the caller is notified when it's done.

before: Method calls block the calling thread until finished
A slow method freezes the entire caller
No way to run multiple requests concurrently, safely
after: Method calls return instantly with a future
Slow work runs on its own thread, never blocking the caller
Requests queue safely without manual thread juggling at each call site

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: The UI freezes for two full seconds every time an image filter runs, mid-click.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Users think the app crashed every time they apply a filter. It's just blocking the UI thread for two seconds.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Scheduler appears holding a ticket dispenser — calls come in instantly, work happens elsewhere.
panels.speaker: The Scheduler
panels.dialogue: Don't run that on the calling thread. Hand me the request — I'll queue it and run it on my own thread instead.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: applyFilter() enqueues a request and returns a Future immediately. A worker thread processes the queue.
panels.speaker: The Scheduler
panels.dialogue: You get your ticket instantly. The UI thread is free the whole time — I'll notify you the moment it's actually done.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The UI stays responsive throughout every filter operation.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Users can click around freely while filters process in the background. No more frozen UI.

useWhen: You need to keep a critical thread (like the UI thread) responsive while expensive work happens elsewhere.
Multiple callers need to safely queue requests to an object without manually managing threads or locks themselves.
You want method calls to return immediately with a future/promise rather than blocking.
avoidWhen: The work is fast enough that synchronous execution never actually blocks anything meaningfully.
You're in a single-threaded environment with cooperative async (like JavaScript's event loop) where a simpler async function already solves the problem.
The overhead of queueing and scheduling outweighs the benefit for your actual workload.
commonMistakes: Adding Active Object's machinery in environments (like Node.js) where async/await already provides non-blocking behavior without a dedicated thread.
Letting the request queue grow unbounded under heavy load, silently consuming memory instead of applying backpressure.
Forgetting proper error handling in the worker loop, letting one failed request silently kill the whole processing thread.
Not making the shared state between the scheduler and the worker properly synchronized, reintroducing the concurrency bugs the pattern exists to prevent.
explanation.realWorldExample: GUI frameworks running expensive work off the UI thread, actor-model systems (like Akka) where each actor processes its own mailbox sequentially, and background job processors decoupling task submission from execution are all Active Object in spirit.

conversation.speaker: The Scheduler
conversation.message: In cooperative single-threaded environments, async/await often gives you enough of my benefit already. I matter most in true multi-threaded environments, where I own an actual dedicated thread and safely serialize access to it.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: What's the real cost of using me?

conversation.speaker: The Scheduler
conversation.message: Complexity. Queueing, scheduling, futures, error propagation across threads — none of it is free. Reach for me when blocking is a real, measured problem, not by default.

codeBattle.scenario: Your desktop app's UI freezes every time a user exports a large file, because the export logic runs synchronously on the same thread that handles clicks and redraws.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Scheduler moves the export work onto its own thread and returns a future immediately, keeping the UI thread free to handle clicks and redraws throughout.

quiz.question: What does Active Object decouple?
options: The moment a method is called from the moment it actually executes
An object's data from its behavior
quiz.answer: The moment a method is called from the moment it actually executes
quiz.explanation: That's the defining move — calling returns instantly, while execution happens later on a dedicated thread.

quiz.question: What does an Active Object typically return immediately to the caller?
options: A future/promise representing the eventual result
quiz.answer: A future/promise representing the eventual result
quiz.explanation: The caller gets something to await or check later, without blocking on the actual work.

quiz.question: When is Active Object likely unnecessary?
options: In a cooperative single-threaded async environment where async/await already avoids blocking
In a UI application where expensive work must not block the interface thread
In a multi-threaded server handling many concurrent requests to one shared object
When you need requests to queue safely without manual thread management at each call site
quiz.answer: In a cooperative single-threaded async environment where async/await already avoids blocking
quiz.explanation: Where async/await already solves the blocking problem, Active Object's dedicated-thread machinery is often redundant.

quiz.question: What's a real risk of Active Object's request queue?
options: It can grow unbounded under heavy load if there's no backpressure
It can never hold more than one request at a time
It requires a database to function
quiz.answer: It can grow unbounded under heavy load if there's no backpressure
quiz.explanation: Without limits or backpressure, a queue accepting requests faster than they're processed will keep growing.
